Part 01Learning section 02

Anatomical orientation, planes and motion

Start with a fixed reference

The anatomical position is the reference used to describe all body directions regardless of how the patient is actually positioned: an erect body, feet together, upper limbs at the sides, and palms facing anteriorly. Supine means lying on the back; prone means face down. A patient can be supine while a structure is still described as anterior in the anatomical reference frame.

Anatomical planes

Plane Divides the body into Practical clinical view
Median (midsagittal) Equal right and left halves Central plane along the midline
Sagittal Right and left portions Any plane parallel to the midline
Frontal (coronal) Anterior and posterior portions Side-to-side partition
Transverse (axial) Superior and inferior portions Cross-sectional CT or axial MRI

Common trap: every median plane is sagittal, but not every sagittal plane is median. The frontal plane is perpendicular to the sagittal plane.

Locations and laterality

Medial means toward the midline; lateral means away. Median refers to the midline itself. Proximal is nearer the origin or limb attachment; distal is farther away. Superior (cranial/cephalic) is toward the head and inferior (caudal) toward the feet. Anterior (ventral) is toward the front, posterior (dorsal) toward the back; superficial is nearer the surface and deep farther in. Ipsilateral means on the same side; contralateral means opposite; bilateral means paired on both sides.

Name the movement precisely

  • Flexion / extension: generally decrease / increase the angle between body parts. At the knee, the relationship of the moving segment to the anterior/posterior direction is different than at the hip; do not substitute forward motion for the precise definition.
  • Abduction / adduction: move away from / toward the median plane (or relevant reference axis for digits).
  • Elevation / depression: raise / lower a structure, such as the scapula.
  • Supination / pronation: in the anatomical reference frame, supination positions the forearm with the palm anteriorly; pronation turns it posteriorly.
  • Dorsiflexion / plantarflexion: bring toes toward the anterior leg / point the foot downward.

Apply it: The radius is lateral to the ulna in anatomical position; a forearm that is pronated changes the bones' spatial relationship, not the underlying anatomical naming convention.

ACTIVE RECALL: A cross-sectional scan passes horizontally through the knee; which plane is it? A lesion is farther from the skin than another lesion; which directional term applies? Answer: transverse/axial; deep.

Part 02Learning section 03

Integument and fascia

The lecture introduces skin because it, together with fascia, provides the superficial layers through which clinicians dissect or examine deeper musculoskeletal structures.

Layer Composition What it means clinically
Epidermis Tough outer cellular layer; avascular Nutrients diffuse from the dermis; superficial burns involve this layer
Dermis Strong collagen and elastic fiber network Contains vessels, sensory endings, follicles, sweat glands, and arrector pili muscles
Subcutaneous tissue / superficial fascia / hypodermis Fat and loose connective tissue Contains superficial vessels and nerves; mobile over deep tissues
Deep fascia Dense, organized connective tissue Encloses muscles and gives rise to investing fascia and intermuscular septa

Skin ligaments extend through subcutaneous tissue to anchor dermis to underlying fascia. Fascial compartments group muscles of related function and often common innervation. Dense septa resist expansion, explaining why increased pressure within a closed compartment can endanger perfusion and nerve function (BOARD / CLINICAL ENRICHMENT: acute compartment syndrome).

LECTURE CLINICAL NOTE — burns: Superficial injury is limited to the epidermis. Partial-thickness injury extends into dermis and can be extremely painful. Full-thickness injury destroys epidermis and dermis and may require grafting. Fourth-degree injury continues into deeper fascia, muscle, or bone. The lecture handout emphasizes that total body surface area is an important determinant of systemic severity, independent of depth.

LECTURE CLINICAL NOTE — surgical planes: Fascial planes provide potential spaces that surgeons can follow; they can also channel or limit infection. Always connect compartment anatomy with neurovascular structures at risk.

ACTIVE RECALL: Why doesn't an isolated epidermal scrape bleed immediately from intrinsic epidermal capillaries? The epidermis contains no blood vessels; bleeding requires injury to vascularized tissue below.

Part 03Learning section 04

Blood vessels, anastomoses and lymphatics

Arteries versus veins

Artery is defined by movement of blood away from the heart, not by oxygen content. Vein means toward the heart, not necessarily deoxygenated blood. Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood away from the heart, while pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to it.

Typical feature Artery Vein
Wall Thicker, maintains a more open lumen Thinner, collapses more readily
Valves Generally absent along systemic arteries Common in peripheral veins
Gross anatomy Often branches at wider angles May pair alongside an artery (venae comitantes)
Direction Away from heart Toward heart

On dissection, nerves tend to be relatively tough and fibrous and branch at acute angles. Arteries, veins, and accompanying nerves can share a neurovascular bundle and vascular sheath. Clinical implication: a traumatic wound or surgical approach can threaten several structures at once.

Anastomosis versus collateral circulation

An anastomosis is the anatomical connection between blood vessels; collateral circulation is functional alternative perfusion through connections when a primary path becomes obstructed. The shoulder and elbow have clinically useful periarticular anastomoses. An existing connection does not guarantee that collateral blood flow is sufficient during an acute complete occlusion; time and vessel caliber matter (BOARD / CLINICAL ENRICHMENT).

Lymphatic return

Lymph is excess interstitial fluid containing escaped plasma proteins, cellular debris, immune cells and potentially microbes. Thin-walled lymphatic vessels collect this material, guide it through lymph nodes for immune filtering, and eventually return it to the venous circulation, chiefly through the thoracic and right lymphatic ducts. The lymphatic system both preserves fluid balance and supports immune surveillance.

Apply it: Swelling after lymph-node dissection is a lymph-drainage problem rather than proof of arterial inflow failure. Distinguish lymphedema from venous obstruction using the history and distribution (BOARD / CLINICAL ENRICHMENT).

ACTIVE RECALL: The pulmonary artery is an artery despite carrying what kind of blood? Deoxygenated, because direction of flow determines naming.

Part 04Learning section 05

Bones, cartilage and joints

Axial versus appendicular

The axial skeleton comprises head, neck, and trunk bones; the appendicular skeleton comprises the limbs plus pectoral and pelvic girdles. The lecture gives a typical adult count of 206 bones and states 177 participate in movement. The skeleton supports weight, transmits muscular force as levers, protects organs and the CNS, stores calcium/phosphate and lipids, and houses blood-cell production.

Wolff's law

Bone is dynamic: mechanical loading alters its structure and internal architecture over time. This is Wolff's law—adaptation to imposed stress, not instantaneous strengthening. The handout offers examples involving adolescent spinal curvature and throwing-related humeral retroversion; remember these as illustrations of adaptation, not evidence that every deformity is caused by load alone.

Recognize bone classes

  • Long: tubular shaft and expanded ends, e.g., humerus and femur. Diaphysis = shaft; metaphysis = expanded transition; epiphysis = end; epiphyseal plate = cartilaginous growth site in immature bone.
  • Short: carpal and tarsal bones; generally cuboidal.
  • Flat: protect underlying tissues, such as ribs and cranial vault.
  • Irregular: complex structures such as vertebrae.
  • Sesamoid: within tendons where they pass a joint, e.g., patella; can alter mechanical advantage.

Ligament connects bone to bone or cartilage; tendon links muscle to bone; aponeurosis is a broad, flat tendon. The innervated periosteum is a major source of pain with fractures or traction.

Cartilage types

Hyaline offers low-friction joint surfaces and growth-plate support; elastic bends and recovers, as in the external ear; fibrocartilage resists compressive and tensile loads, as in intervertebral discs and pubic symphysis. These examples explain the three categories introduced in the lecture.

Three structural classes of joints

Class Characteristic connection Examples
Synovial Capsule, inner synovial membrane, synovial fluid-filled space, articular cartilage Shoulder, knee
Fibrous Bones united by strong fibrous tissue Skull sutures, radioulnar interosseous membrane
Cartilaginous Bones joined by hyaline cartilage or fibrocartilage Growth plate, pubic symphysis, intervertebral disc

Six types of synovial joints (know the movement, axis, and an example): plane = gliding (acromioclavicular), hinge = flexion/extension (elbow), pivot = rotation (atlantoaxial), condyloid = two-plane motion (metacarpophalangeal), saddle = two-axis motion (thumb carpometacarpal), ball-and-socket = multiaxial motion (hip, shoulder).

ACTIVE RECALL: Which joint type would you expect between skull bones? Fibrous suture. Which synovial type permits rotation at C1–C2? Pivot. Why is the patella sesamoid? It develops in a tendon and modifies leverage.

Part 05Learning section 06

Skeletal muscles, compartments and contraction

Three muscle tissues

Skeletal muscle is striated, mainly voluntary, attached to body structures and generates movement. Smooth muscle is nonstriated, involuntary and forms much of the walls of vessels and hollow viscera. Cardiac muscle is striated but involuntary and specialized for coordinated pumping in the heart.

The unifying output: tension

The lecture emphasizes that the direct mechanical output of muscle is tension, from which movement, posture, joint stability, visceral support, intracavity pressure regulation, and heat production result. Muscles can be active while joint position remains unchanged.

Irritability (excitability) = responsiveness to stimulation; contractility = ability to develop active tension, often producing shortening; extensibility = capacity to stretch; elasticity = return toward resting length after stretching. The handout emphasizes the role of connective tissue in extensibility and recoil. Muscle force also reflects fiber size, architecture, neural activation, contractile speed, and current length.

Compare contraction types using torque

Contraction Muscle behavior Relationship between joint torques Example
Isometric Active tension with no net length change / joint movement Internal and external torques balance Holding a dumbbell motionless
Concentric Active muscle shortens Internal muscle torque exceeds opposing external torque Raising a dumbbell by flexing elbow
Eccentric Active muscle lengthens under load Opposing external torque exceeds muscle torque, with controlled motion Lowering a dumbbell slowly

Exam trap: The biceps can act as an agonist during both lifting and controlled lowering: in the latter, the biceps remains active but undergoes eccentric action. The direction of motion alone does not determine which muscle is generating tension. The professor's slide 26 invites this exact analysis.

Agonists, antagonists and synergists

An agonist is the principal muscle or group producing the required torque; an antagonist produces opposing action; synergists work cooperatively. Two special synergist roles are neutralizers (counter an undesired secondary action) and stabilizers (hold a segment so intended movement occurs). The handout's example: trapezius and rhomboids can cooperate in scapular retraction while opposing aspects of scapular rotation; gluteus medius stabilizes the pelvis during single-leg stance.

ACTIVE RECALL: During controlled descent from an elbow curl, is biceps silent? No—it typically generates eccentric tension. During knee extension, quadriceps is usually agonist and hamstrings antagonist.

Part 06Learning section 07

Torque, strength and musculoskeletal levers

From force to rotation

A muscle's action is its potential to create torque about a joint axis in a given plane. The muscle's line of pull and the joint's axis of rotation determine the turning effect, so the same muscle may have different moment arms or secondary actions in different joint positions.

[ ext{Torque}= ext{Force} imes ext{moment arm}]

The moment arm is the shortest perpendicular distance from the joint's rotation axis to the force's line of action. Doubling force at the same moment arm doubles torque; decreasing the perpendicular distance reduces torque even if muscle force stays constant. The handout specifically stresses that insertion angle and attachment point matter and that the moment arm usually changes through range of motion. A muscle can be strongest at a joint angle that is not its most shortened position because both muscle force and leverage vary.

Muscle force determinants identified in the lecture: muscle size and architecture; fiber types; motor-unit recruitment and rate coding; length–tension relationship; force–velocity relationship. These factors are named here, while the handout notes that later lectures will deepen the physiology.

Three classes of lever

Treat each movable joint system as fulcrum (F), load (L) and effort (E).

Lever class Middle element Anatomical example Mechanical tradeoff
Class 1 Fulcrum between effort and load: E–F–L Neck extensors balancing head May favor force or speed depending on distances
Class 2 Load between fulcrum and effort: F–L–E Heel raise / triceps surae Mechanical advantage; favor force over load travel
Class 3 Effort between fulcrum and load: F–E–L Biceps flexing the forearm Disadvantage for force; favors load speed and range

Class 3 is most common in human joints. This is not poor design: the small shortening of a muscle can translate to large distal movement. A class 2 lever gives an advantage for lifting a heavy load but sacrifices distance and speed, given similar configurations.

Worked biomechanical example

A muscle exerts 200 N with a perpendicular moment arm of 0.03 m. Its joint torque is 6 N·m. When the moment arm increases to 0.04 m with the same force, the torque rises to 8 N·m. These are teaching examples (BOARD / CLINICAL ENRICHMENT), not measurements claimed by the lecture.

ACTIVE RECALL: In the biceps curl, which lies between the elbow fulcrum and the load at the hand? The biceps effort: class 3. During a heel raise, which is between forefoot fulcrum and calf effort? Body-weight load: class 2.

Learning section 08

Integrated clinical reasoning

Case A — interpreting a limb examination

A patient reports pain in the lateral forearm. The examiner performs elbow flexion and extension while tracking muscle activity. Describe the location with reference to anatomical position, identify the elbow as a hinge-type synovial joint, and explain why the biceps can remain active during a slow lowering motion.

Reasoning: Lateral refers to the radial side in anatomical position. Hinge joints primarily support flexion/extension. With controlled elbow extension under a heavy external load, the biceps can develop tension while lengthening—an eccentric contraction. The direction of movement and the agonist's contraction type are not identical concepts.

Case B — anatomy in a deep injury

After a penetrating extremity injury, a clinician encounters a collapsible thin-walled structure, a firmer thick-walled tubular structure, and a tough fibrous cord nearby. Identify these anatomical classes and explain why injury to one region can affect movement and sensation simultaneously.

Reasoning: The first suggests vein; second suggests artery; third suggests nerve. Co-travel within neurovascular bundles makes simultaneous vascular and neurologic injury possible. Gross appearance guides identification but clinical assessment remains essential.

Case C — force and leverage

A patient can produce muscular tension yet fails to elevate a load. What could be wrong even if the muscle is contracting?

Reasoning: Joint motion requires net joint torque, not simply the presence of muscle contraction. Muscle force and moment arm together determine internal torque, opposed by gravity and external resistance. Isometric equilibrium may occur when the torques balance.

Learning section 09

MASTER THESE BEFORE MOVING ON

  • Describe anatomical position without reference to how a patient happens to lie.
  • Distinguish sagittal, median, coronal and axial planes and localize proximal/distal/medial/lateral.
  • Differentiate epidermis, dermis, superficial fascia and deep fascia; explain their clinical significance.
  • Name arteries and veins by flow direction and identify the pulmonary exceptions.
  • Explain anastomosis, collateral circulation, lymph vessels and lymph nodes.
  • Classify axial/appendicular bones; list long/short/flat/irregular/sesamoid types.
  • Recognize fibrous, cartilaginous, synovial joints and all six synovial subclasses.
  • Compare skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle and four muscle properties.
  • Recognize isometric, concentric and eccentric actions in an actual movement.
  • Label agonists, antagonists, neutralizers and stabilizers in specific tasks.
  • Calculate torque using perpendicular moment arm; identify class 1/2/3 levers.
Learning section 10

THE MOST USEFUL FIRST AID CONNECTIONS

These are FIRST AID CONNECTION / BOARD-STYLE cross-links consistent with standard Step 1 anatomy and physiology topics; they are supplementary context, not claims that every example is written in the lecture. The uploaded First Aid 2025 is a reference for this project.

  1. Compartment syndrome: Fascial anatomy explains why pressure rises within relatively noncompliant compartments and can compromise local perfusion. Relate acute severe pain and pain with passive stretch to deep compartment injury.
  2. Joint disease: The synovial capsule, synovial membrane and articular hyaline cartilage are distinct tissues affected differently by inflammation and degeneration.
  3. Bone growth and loading: Metaphysis, epiphysis and epiphyseal plate give the spatial vocabulary needed for pediatric injury and growth-plate disorders; Wolff's law introduces load adaptation.
  4. Clinical nerve/vascular examination: An artery, vein and nerve may travel together. Understanding adjacent structures helps localize injury patterns.
  5. Lymphedema versus vascular edema: Tissue fluid return via lymphatics is anatomically distinct from arterial delivery and venous drainage.
  6. Muscle contraction: Isometric/concentric/eccentric categories concern what an active muscle does relative to the external load, not merely which direction the limb moves.
  7. Force/lever mechanics: Biceps uses a third-class lever to generate speed/range; calf raise demonstrates a second-class lever's force advantage.
